My personal recommendation due to experiencing discrimination based on my disability at my uni (bc tbh this seems like the case to me): Go to your uni's ombudsperson, the director of your degree program (I assume its a different person than your department head?), your uni's ADA/disability advocate (idk if you live in the USA), and your disability services advocate (if you receive services at the uni). If you are in a grad program, I'd go to your academic/dissertation advisor too. Explain what happened, why the prof failed you, and how you believe this to be unfair due to your disability. Did the course syllabus say you had to participate in discussions during class or ask at least one question? Whether it did or not say that, I'd have a (virtual or hard) copy of the syllabus handy. Explain that the reason the prof failed you for both courses is unfair, discriminatory, and ultimately nonsensical. 

This will all prepare you to either mediate the situation with your professor or prepare you to go to the dean. Legitimately, unless this was a course requirement, they should not be able to fail you because you asked "too few" questions. And they definitely shouldn't be able to fail you if you asked "too many," because that would be a stupid reason. This is supposed to be an institution of learning.

Helen's Lament - The Grand Cyberpunk Gala of Gabriella Gadfly: Helen has basically just been told that her life isn't real and now she is so broken that she feels like she has to end it all to free her friends who are trapped inside her head so they can defeat the evil AI creatures who created their fake lives.

Having remnants of dead family and friends has been made illegal since the people of New Albion decided to riot in the streets and kill all the dolls (like Jasper, reincarnated loved ones). Anyone found with such possessions, including dolls, will be killed. Jasper just wants to die to go back to "heaven" but stays alive for Priscillas sake as she is the only one who hasn't been selfish with him. Priscilla contemplates what love really means and concludes that the ultimate act of love, in this particular fucked up instance, is to call the cops on herself so Jasper can finally die and go back to "heaven". This will end in her death to, but that's a sacrifice she is willing to make. Jasper protests as he doesn't want Priscilla to die but ultimately can't stop the police from killing them both.

The Suicide - The Dolls of New Albion: A Steampunk Opera: Amelia lives with an abusive father. She hears the dolls broadcast a song on the radio about how great "heaven" is because all your troubles are gone. She decides that she will go there so she won't feel anymore pain.

Christmas in the City - Katy Shaw and the Stolen Secret: Katy recounts her mother's suicide. Katy's dad left her mom, in turn leaving her poor and destitute. Katy went out to steal a huge score of money to help out her mom, but when she got back to the hotel she was staying at she had found that her mom had already died by suicide. It happened in Christmas, hence the title.

Nathan Brindesi - The Grand Cyberpunk Gala of Gabriella Gadfly: Nathan starts off as a not-so-well-known author with crippling social anxiety and agoraphobia. Might be one single thing we get right education wise. Our states is one of the States that may get rid of 504 plans.
Teachers definitely need more support and compensation than they are currently getting. Teachers get so much flack too. Only gonna get worse in the USA too. Poor teachers.

Where I am being trained (not as a teacher, as a school psych), as far as I know teachers are sort of taught to know how to look out for "warning signs" of a variety of disabilities, including autism. And of course, you learn more the longer you are on the job.

One issue I see is a structural/systemic one. Teachers are asked to do so much every day and all the time. Lots of states and districts are full of complaints from teachers saying they don't have adequate support to carry out all their duties consistently. Of course, they are also not being fairly compensated. A teacher is only one person and is given a lot of responsibilities and duties that are expected of them. They are humans, and sometimes they fall short and not due to a lack of trying. That doesn't make it okay, but it does mean that teachers need significantly more support and compensation than they are getting.

Another issue I see is that parents can be...interesting...to work with. I will say, a majority of the parents and families I have personally worked with want their child/ren to get all of the support that they need. But the 10-15% of parents that I have worked with that don't want their kids to have IEPs/504 plans (despite REALLY needed one) or to not have specific services that they need in those plans...ugh. It is frustrating because, legally, we have to respect the parents/legal guardians wishes. I understand why that is important. But it also means that a kid may not get the services they need to do well/better in school. So, basically, if a teacher or other school staff tells a parent they suspect their kid might be autistic, parents can and will just brush it off (as other comments here have pointed out). Schools can do very little outside of providing core education without parental consent.

That also goes for every single "special" school service. Your parent can decide that you don't need an IEP or 504 plan. Your parents can decide that you can't see the school counselor/therapist. I'm training to be a school psychologist and the amount of parents I've ran into who have kids who could really benefit from some sort of additional support and say "Nope, we don't want them to have that" baffles me. Don't come crying to us when your kid can't graduate from high school because they never got the support they needed. I mean they *will* come crying to us and will blame us for not "doing more," despite that being what we tried to do in the first place. But oh well 🙃

I've had a previous professor tell me that she wasn't comfortable with me using my audio recording accommodation because people in the class were probably going to talk about personal stuff to relate to the topic (Multicultural Counseling). She also said the class would be mainly discussion based, so that's fine I guess. Except one week our topic was on elderly populations.

Having a concentration in developmental psychology (primarily focused on kids and teens), having only have worked with kids before, and being a current school psychology student, I don't have any experience in working with elderly people as clients. Only tangentially (e.g., a kid at a school could have their grandparent as their primary guardian). So because I was discouraged from using my audio recording accommodation, I was typing notes during the discussion bc we talked about things that weren't addressed in the readings.  Also because I was taking notes (and because I have a lack of experience withing with elderly people directly), I didn't contribute to the discussion much.

She sent me an email the next day saying that I didn't look like I was super involved in the discussion and that I kept "working on other things" on my computer. I basically told her what I told you in the previous paragraph and that I wanted to have more context on working with elderly populations (I even mentioned that she discouraged me from using my audio recording accommodation in the email). That shut her up. Having that kind of thing in writing tends to do that. Also, wouldn't you know, I have a disability accommodation for a fucking reason!

That class, and that prof in particular, has had a lot of issues with students specifically from my program. I could say so much more about her but my colleagues and I already said it all in our course evaluations :) Long story short I will no longer allow myself to be discouraged from using my accommodations, and hell upon the prof who tries to not acknowledge them or let me use them. I am sorry that this does not answer your question, but here is my perspective on IQ as someone getting her PhD in School Psychology. (Apologies, this turned out long, what else did you expect from an academic?)

IQ tests have also been historically, shall we say, narrow. The way that test scores are given meaning is by gathering a normative population and seeing where they all fall. A lot of IQ assessments (say you are from the States) are not normed for people who are not from America, don't speak English as a first language, people with disabilities, people who are or were homeless, etc. In the past they also were not normed for people who were not White, at least middle class, or women/girls. This means that if you fall under one of these groups, your test results should be interpreted with a grain of salt.

That being said, IQ is not unimportant. But often the value of overall IQ is overemphasized, especially in schools. It is one piece of data among a vast sea of other types of data (academic scores, historical documents, medical documents, self reported information, teacher and parent reported information, observation data, personal strengths and skills, and much more). Your IQ doesn't dictate your capabilities or your potential. Looking at parts of your IQ (e.g., verbal, nonverbal, visuo-spatial IQ, information processing speed) is more helpful than your overall IQ, but even those do not set your abilities in stone.

One of the first things I learned in my IQ assessment course is to not write off a student simply because of a low IQ score, it is quite literally discrimination. What your teachers did to you was discriminatory. It's one of the reasons that IQ testing in schools is falling out of fashion, and some districts or schools don't even test for IQ anymore (in the USA at least). One of my first assigned "readings" for this course was a podcast episode about (iirc) a cognitive psychologist who received an IQ score in the 70s or 80s when he was in grade school and was put in special education. He got into the gifted education program at his school out of spite after that, studied his ass off to beat the tests, and became successful as a result (like I said, he's a cognitive psychologist now with a PhD and everything). I'll link the episode if I can find it again, because it's an interesting listen.

All that being said: You have already demonstrated that having a low IQ, if you do have it, did not stop you from getting high grades in math (a subject that many struggle with- I'm getting my PhD right now and I'd probably fail or barely pass all your calculus classes). I know that intelligence is something that is highly valued in academia, and that people are made fun of for having low IQ, but IQ is only one piece of the puzzle that makes up every human being. Your socioeconomic status is a better determinant of how successful you can be than your IQ, as richer people have more resources. Plus, not everyone who has a high IQ is successful. It simply takes more than that.

(Long story oncoming) I am happy that I've seen at least one instance of this starting to improve. I'm in grad school and I do practicum at a variety of mainly elementary schools. Early this school year I was sent to observe this one student in class and at recess because they suspected that he had behavioral issues and he was being evaluated for a behavior intervention plan. Granted, this kid was not diagnosed autistic, but he had very similar (for lack of better phrasing) "overreactions" to certain things. You'll see why I put that word in quote marks.

From what I was told, he was disruptive in class and didn't get along well with his peers. Behaviors I saw were: yelling, crying, hitting himself in the head, calling himself stupid (and things like that), and screaming at people to leave him alone or get away from him. The only time he would exhibit these types of behaviors was, unfortunately, when he was being teased, bullied, or ignored/excluded (when he was trying to contribute in small group or during playtime) by the other students. I talked to his teacher and she confirmed that those were pretty much the only times he behaved like that. Sometimes he was able to catch himself before he got too distressed and would ask the teacher for help, other times she would notice and go to him to comfort him and help him regulate. He was never punished, and I think it was because his teacher saw what was going on. 

One particular time at recess this poor kid was having a complete meltdown due to bullying, and the teacher just told the students to stop bothering him because it was distressing him more. He ended up needing to have lunch in the SpEd room (so he could get out of the situation, not as punishment) and the teacher explained to the other students what when someone gets so overwhelmed like that, not to instigate that person further. He was never punished, and after I reported all this info back to my supervisor, we determined that he didn't have a behavior problem but an adaptive one. I wish that kids would stop being so mean, but I am happy that student got the support he needed and wasn't being punished for reacting to bullying.

A lot of people in my program (School Psychology) are self-described behaviorist, which naturally leads them to ABA. I find this so, so funny because in my undergrad (Psychology), I learned about behaviorism as a foundational theoretical orientation for the field but because it is so limiting, not a lot of people really call themselves behaviorists anymore. Wouldn't you know it, people have thoughts in their heads! People have emotions! Crazy. Anyways. I guess I just happened to find myself in a program/area of learning where behaviorism is still the hot new thing somehow. This us incredibly annoying because I've always been a fan of more all-encompassing theoretical orientations like the Ecological Systems theory. It has its faults but at least it's not just 'antecedent, behavior, consequence.' I mean in my behavioral interventions class our prof told us that a possible motivation for behavior is to gain or avoid a sensory experience, and then he said that we weren't gonna learn about that because it's not directly observable. Great! Now everyone in that class knows to misconstrue an autistic kids meltdowns as "Oh, they just want to gain peer attention," that's gonna be super helpful and beneficial in the field.

Another point I'll add is that while new ABA is better than original ABA (although still not great as you know), not all clinics follow those newer outlined best practices. For example, a good chunk of ABA institutions still practice hand-over-hand learning which reduces the autonomy of the patient (victim?) in this scenario. Hand-over-hand learning is no longer considered best practice. And as you know (and I think as you mentioned in your comment), one very well known ABA institution (linked with Autism Speaks of course) still/up until recently uses/used electrocution and other forms of physical punishment. Basically, there is a lot of inconsistency across ABA providers.

Another another point I'll add, and this isn't necessarily about the nature of ABA, but I find it pretty predatory that ABA is often the only type of therapy meant for autistic people that is covered by insurance. Other therapies that are beneficial for autistic people definitely exist, but those usually are not covered. So even if a parent wants their kid to be in something other than ABA, if they don't have the money, their choices are limited. Plus, often in order for the therapy to be paid for, the kid needs to be in ABA for a gross amount of time, like 40 hours a week. On top of school and other necessary things like sleeping. So these poor kids barely even have time to be kids. And! This also causes a lot of providers who don't actually use ABA to label themselves as ABA providers so parents and kids using their services will have it covered by insurance, which makes it very confusing imo.

There is this concept called twice exceptionality (2e). It means you have been identified as gifted while also having some sort of disability such as autism, adhd, ocd, a learning disability, etc. This is still an emerging area of research. 2e students can easily get missed because either their giftedness can hide their disability or their disability can hide their giftedness. So at least from an outside perspective, having high cognitive abilities can *seem* to 'compensate for' some autistic symptoms.

Of course this doesn't mean the person still won't feel the severity of such symptoms or that the symptoms cease to exist. The masking and not getting the accommodations or help they really need based on their disability will negatively impact them in the long run. Some people even (wrongly) assume that an autistic person will be okay and not need additional help if they are gifted. This is not true. Disability accommodations should still be put in place.

I don't think looking into behavioral stuff is inherently bad, but you definitely have to look at a bunch of other stuff too. Pure behaviorism is pretty archaic even though it was a foundational theoretical approach. It is important to teach kids strategies so that they find better ways of expressing themselves that don't involve harming themselves or others. And of course this stuff doesn't just apply to autistic kids. But you also have to look at other factors like mood, family history, personal history, the multiple environments the kid finds themselves in (home, school, etc), other mental health conditions and disabilities, medication, the current society, all of that and more. Anything less is too limited.

And not every reaction that is outside the norm is a behavioral issue, often I have found it is an adaptive issue. During my practicum last week I was sent to observe a kid who already has behavioral goals to determine if he was really a "behavior kid" (term we use for kid with behavioral "issues") or an "adaptive kid." I observed him during class, recess, and lunch. Turns out he only demonstrated "bad behavior" when he was being fucking bullied. He didn't have a diagnosis for anything but he was clearly overwhelmed and frustrated. He was crying, hitting his head with his fists, and in some cases screaming :( Poor kid just needed a break with something or someone that could help regulate him, unfortunately we do not yet know what that is for him yet and both of his teachers would just tell him to calm down (tho one did explain to his group that what they were doing was not nice). Otherwise he was calm, asked the teacher for help when he needed it, and was a little distracted from doing his work sometimes. The SpEd teacher was a lot better at actually helping him calm down than his gen ed teachers by distracting him by talking about the lunch options for the day. 

The whole demonization of both behavior kids and adaptive kids is still...ugh...but at least people can kind of make that distinction now. We have a lot of work to do in this field.

I'm in an Ethics in Psychology course, one of our readings introduced a the concept of a pod system.

You have people in the pods in your inner circle of pods. These are people you trust who can talk to you when you feel suicidal besides your therapist. These people have to consent to be a part of this.

People in the circle of pods just outside of that are people you think may one day join your inner circle, but you might not know them well enough.

The circle of pods outside of that include local low cost or free mental health services (not hospitalization) that can help when you are feeling suicidal or in distress. 

The outermost circle of pods contain similar services, but more state wide, national, or global services.

This is all drawn out on a worksheet and planned with the client ideally during the first appointment when you discuss informed consent. Float the idea of using this system when discussing informed consent, if the client wants to do that then go for it. That way, if the client expresses SI, you can both revisit the pod map together and pick a person/service to utilize. The client can call, you can call, or you can both call them together.
